To fix (3)

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 32 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p < 0.05 The calculation used p < 0.05 and 90% power giving a target sample size of 503 participants.

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 10 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = 0.777 Responses to the two ambiguous stimuli (Ambiguous Negative and Ambiguous Positive) were compared using a paired-samples t-test, the assumptions of which were met; a Shapiro-Wilk test indicated that the difference scores did not deviate from normality (W = 0.998, p = 0.777) supported by visual inspection of the histogram and Q-Q plots.
p = 0.055 No significant difference in ‘optimistic’ responses between the Ambiguous Negative and Ambiguous Positive stimuli was found in post-hoc comparisons of our trial-level analysis (z = 2.496, p = 0.055; see supplementary material).
p = 0.310 The effects of anxiety (LRT = 1.031, p = 0.310), depression (LRT = 0.493, p = 0.483), and pessimism (LRT = 0.153, p = 0.696) on Optimistic Responses were not significant in this model.
p = 0.483 The effects of anxiety (LRT = 1.031, p = 0.310), depression (LRT = 0.493, p = 0.483), and pessimism (LRT = 0.153, p = 0.696) on Optimistic Responses were not significant in this model.
p = 0.696 The effects of anxiety (LRT = 1.031, p = 0.310), depression (LRT = 0.493, p = 0.483), and pessimism (LRT = 0.153, p = 0.696) on Optimistic Responses were not significant in this model.

p = 0.570 There was no significant effect of sex on threshold separation (LRT = 2.013, p = 0.570).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. setwd() calls were found in 13 code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 2 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 25 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A package could not be installed.

  • EXP1_HDDM_25_516.ipynb needs hddm.
  • EXP1_HDDM_holdout.ipynb needs hddm.
  • EXP1_HDDM_parameter_recovery_participantlevel.ipynb needs hddm.
  • OE1 age and sex plots.R needs raincloudplots.

hddm could not be installed with the current version of R, probably because it is old. Record the versions you used (in R, renv::init() writes them to a renv.lock file) and your R version. To be sure the code keeps running, provide a Docker image: a frozen copy of the whole computer setup the code needs, which you can build from rocker/r-ver at your R version.

raincloudplots could not be installed with the current version of R, probably because it is old. Record the versions you used (in R, renv::init() writes them to a renv.lock file) and your R version. To be sure the code keeps running, provide a Docker image: a frozen copy of the whole computer setup the code needs, which you can build from rocker/r-ver at your R version.

A script uses something it does not create or load itself.

  • Trial_level_analysis.R: Trial.Number

Usually the object was still in your R session from earlier work, or another script made it.

  1. Restart R (in RStudio: Session > Restart R).
  2. Run each script from top to bottom, and fix what is missing.
  3. If a script needs results of another, save them to a file in the first script and read them in the second.
  4. Load every package with library() at the top.

Undefined-variable errors

1 script failed on an undefined variable or function (object '...' not found / could not find function "..."). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper’s own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

File Missing variable Defined in
Trial_level_analysis.R Trial.Number (not defined anywhere in the paper’s code)

Dependency-unavailable errors

1 script could not run because its own dependency is unavailable — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so it does not force the traffic light red.

File
OE1 age and sex plots.R

setwd() in the code

13 scripts call setwd(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring a setwd() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Reproducible after removing setwd(): Calculate_GAD7_score.R, Aim1_analysis.R, Tidy_demo_questionnaire_data.R, Aim2_analysis.R, Prep_data_for_HDDM.R, Calculate_PHQ8_score.R, Calculate_LOTRP_score.R, Plot_Prop_op.R, Process_HDDM_output.R.

> filtered_data$Response <- as.numeric(filtered_data$Response)
> dframe1 <- filtered_data %>%

> df_pes <- dframe1 %>%
>   filter(Question.Key %in% c("LOTRQ3_wrong-quantised", "LOTRQ7_my_way-quantised", "LOTRQ9_good_things-quantised"))
> df_op <- dframe1 %>%
>   filter(Question.Key %in% c("LOTRQ1_uncertain-quantised", "LOTRQ4_optimistic-quantised", "LOTRQ10_overall_good-quantised"))
> df_op$Response_corrected <- ((df_op$Response*-1)+6)
> df_op = select(df_op, -Response)
> df_op <- df_op %>% 
>   rename(Response = Response_corrected)
> combined_df <- rbind(df_pes, df_op)
> combined_df$Response <- (combined_df$Response-1)
> df_total <- combined_df %>%
>   group_by(Participant.Private.ID) %>%
>   summarise(LOTRP = sum(Response))
> write.csv(df_total,"EXP1_LOTRP_scores.csv", row.names = FALSE)

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

In a pre-registered online experiment, participants completed questionnaires assessing anxiety, depression, and pessimism, and undertook a judgement bias task.

These translational tasks were originally developed for use with animals, on the basis of findings from human psychology that people with mood disorders, or in induced negative affective states, interpreted ambiguous words, phrases, facial expressions, and future scenarios more negatively (e.g. Eysenck et al., 1991; Joormann & Gotlib, 2006; Mathews et al., 1989; Park et al., 2016; Wright & Bower, 1992). In Harding et al.’s (2004) original animal judgement bias task, rats were trained to press a lever when they heard a tone associated with a food reward, and to refrain from pressing the lever when they heard a different tone to avoid a punishment (white noise).

Conversely, if the participant had similar reaction time profiles for both responses but responded ‘pessimistically’ more often, this would be reflected by a negative drift rate (with drift rate = 0 reflecting no drift towards either boundary) and suggest that the negative bias was generated during the decision-making process.

For example, Aylward et al. (2020) used a two-tone discrimination task in which participants had to press one key when a certain tone played to receive a high reward of £4 and had to press another key when a different tone played to receive a low reward of £1.

During testing, participants were also presented with an intermediate ambiguous tone on some trials, and their responses to this ambiguous tone were investigated.

In the task, participants had to decide whether to make the ‘optimistic’ response (the response associated with receiving a high reward) or the ‘pessimistic’ response (the response associated with receiving a low reward) when shown ambiguous visual stimuli.

Participants provided informed consent via an online consent form.

Participants were recruited and reimbursed for their time via Prolific (www.prolific.com).

The inclusion criteria were: (1) individuals over 18 years old, (2) individuals who currently lived in the UK, and (3) individuals who selected ‘United Kingdom’ as their nationality on Prolific.

To encourage engagement with the task, participants were told that they had a chance to earn the 20p bonus depending on whether they responded correctly on one trial selected at random.

To ensure that participants were attending to the possible trial outcomes, they were also told that for every 100 people that completed the task, the best performing participant would receive an extra bonus of £10.

We recruited 540 participants in total, based on a 93% completion rate observed in Daniel-Watanabe et al. (2022). 20 participants withdrew from the study, and data from a further 4 participants were excluded due to poor performance in the task (responding incorrectly on 50% or more of either of the unambiguous stimuli trials).

Participants completed the Generalised Anxiety Disorder Assessment (GAD-7) (Spitzer et al., 2006) to measure anxiety and the Patient Health Questionnaire (PHQ-8) (Kroenke et al., 2001; Wu et al., 2020) to measure depression.

All participants completed the study in a fixed order: consent form, judgement bias task (see below), LOT-R questionnaire, PHQ-8 questionnaire, GAD-7 questionnaire, demographics questionnaire.

Participants were instructed to ensure that they were sat upright, 60cm from the screen and that their screen was level.

To ensure that the stimuli appeared correctly, participants were required to calibrate their screen using Gorilla’s screen calibration function.

Participants were told that the aim of the task was to earn as much money as possible.

Prior to each testing block, participants completed a training block of 20 trials using only the unambiguous stimuli.

During testing participants were also presented with ambiguous patches which were only slightly tilted to the left or right.

In addition, data from 4 participants were excluded due to poor performance in the task (responding incorrectly on 50% or more of either of the unambiguous stimuli trials).

Sex was a significant predictor of Optimistic Responses (LRT = 36.474, p < 0.001); post-hoc analysis revealed that male participants had significantly higher Optimistic Responses than females (male mean: 0.63, female mean: 0.56; z = 5.961, p < 0.001, Figure 4).

Sex was also a 490 significant predictor of drift rate (LRT = 31.364, p < 0.001); post-hoc analysis revealed that male 491 participants had significantly higher drift rates than females (z = 5.515, p < 0.001).

Using a large-scale preregistered online experiment where participants completed questionnaires assessing anxiety, depression, and pessimism, and undertook a judgement bias task, we confirmed that selfreported negative affect is associated with negative judgement biases during decision-making under ambiguity; individuals who reported higher anxiety (GAD-7) and depression (PHQ-8) scores made a significantly lower proportion of ‘optimistic’ responses when faced with ambiguous stimuli in the judgement bias task.

Male participants were also significantly more ‘optimistic’ than females in the task, a finding not observed in Daniel-Watanabe et al.’s (2022) study.

  1. Participants were required to classify Gabor patches as tilted to the left or right of vertical.

Each participant completed 240 trials in total with the four stimuli equally represented. n=516.

Ethics approval statement:

Ethical approval was granted by the University of Bristol Human Research Ethics Committee (Ref: 2020-7982-7929).

Power Analysis Check

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/DeepSeek-V41-Flash-1017-FP8’ to check the contents of 1 paragraph that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

All essential information could be detected.

power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
apriori correlation 503 0.05 0.9 -0.13 other G*Power
text
To determine the target sample size, we used G*Power (v3.1.9.7, Faul et al., 2007) to conduct a power calculation. The power calculation was based on a finding from a similar study (Daniel-Watanabe et al., 2022), where a significant correlation of r=-0.13 was observed between the proportion of ‘optimistic’ responses to ambiguous stimuli in a decision-making task and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) scores. The calculation used p < 0.05 and 90% power giving a target sample size of 503 participants. We recruited 540 participants in total, based on a 93% completion rate observed in Daniel-Watanabe et al. (2022). 20 participants withdrew from the study, and data from a further 4 participants were excluded due to poor performance in the task (responding incorrectly on 50% or more of either of the unambiguous stimuli trials). This gave a final sample size of 516 (273 female; 236 male; 4 other; 3 prefer not to say; aged 18-73; median age = 36 years). Due to the low number of participants reporting their sex as ‘other’ or ‘prefer not to say’, statistical comparisons are only made between participants reporting their sex as ‘male’ or ‘female’. Data from participants reporting their sex as ‘other’ or ‘prefer not to say’ are still included in the analyses.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

research_questions We hypothesise that negative trait affect will be associated with pessimistic decisions to ambiguous stimuli:

1) We predict a negative correlation between pessimism scores (measured using the LOT-R) and the proportion of optimistic responses made for the ambiguous stimuli.

2) We predict a negative correlation between anxiety symptom scores (measured using the GAD-7) and the proportion of optimistic responses made for the ambiguous stimuli.

3) We predict a negative correlation between depression symptom scores (measured using the PHQ-8) and the proportion of optimistic responses made for the ambiguous stimuli.

data_collection_procedures We will run an online experiment using Gorilla (https://gorilla.sc/). Participants will be recruited and reimbursed for their time via Prolific (https://www.prolific.co/). The inclusion criteria are individuals over 18 years old who live in the UK. The whole experiment should take around 20 minutes to complete and participants will be paid £1.80 for their time plus a bonus of 20p. To encourage engagement with the task participants will be told that they have a chance to earn the 20p bonus depending on whether they respond correctly on one trial selected at random. All participants will receive the 20p bonus regardless of performance. To ensure that participants are attending to the possible trial outcomes, they will be told that for every 100 people that complete the task, the best performing participant will receive an extra bonus of £10.

Daniel-Watanabe, L., McLaughlin, M., Gormley, S., & Robinson, O. (2020). Association Between a Directly Translated Cognitive Measure of Negative Bias and Self-reported Psychiatric Symptoms. Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience And Neuroimaging. doi: 10.1016/j.bpsc.2020.02.010
sample_size_rationale We used GPower (Faul et al., 2007) to conduct a power calculation. The power calculation was based on a finding from a similar study (Daniel- Watanabe et al., 2020), where a correlation of r=-0.13 was observed between the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli in a decision-making task and Beck Depression Inventory (BDI) scores. The calculation used p < 0.05 and 90% power.


Daniel-Watanabe, L., McLaughlin, M., Gormley, S., & Robinson, O. (2020). Association Between a Directly Translated Cognitive Measure of Negative Bias and Self-reported Psychiatric Symptoms. Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience And Neuroimaging. doi: 10.1016/j.bpsc.2020.02.010
Faul, F., Erdfelder, E., Lang, A., & Buchner, A. (2007). GPower 3: A flexible statistical power analysis program for the social, behavioral, and biomedical sciences. Behavior Research Methods, 39(2), 175-191. doi: 10.3758/bf03193146
measured_variables Participants will complete several questionnaires as well as a decision-making task. The task will involve classifying Gabor patch images of various orientations as leaning to the left or the right by making keyboard press responses (‘z’ for left, ‘m’ for right). There will be two unambiguous stimuli (-3.2 and 3.2 degrees from vertical) and two ambiguous stimuli (-0.05 and 0.05 degrees from vertical). Correct responses will be rewarded with either a high reward (£4) or low reward (£1) depending on the Gabor patch orientation (left or right) and participants will receive £0 for an incorrect response. Participants will be told that the aim of the experiment is to win as much money as possible.

The high/low reward direction will be counterbalanced within a participant to account for any directional bias i.e. where a participant is predisposed to select either the left or right key, regardless of the stimulus. Participants will therefore complete 2 testing blocks, one where left-leaning patches are rewarded with £4 and one where left-leaning patches are rewarded with £1 (and vice versa for right-leaning patches). Both testing blocks will consist of 120 trials with all four stimuli equally represented across testing trials in a fixed random order. Prior to each testing block, participants will complete a training block of 20 trials using only the unambiguous stimuli. Only data from the testing blocks will be included in the analysis.

The key outcome of interest is the proportion of optimistic responses for the ambiguous stimuli. Here we define an optimistic response as the response associated with the high-reward (£4) direction.

Variables measured from questionnaires:
• Pessimism score, measured using the Revised Life Orientation Test (LOT-R)
• Anxiety symptoms score, measured using the Generalised Anxiety Disorder Assessment (GAD-7)
• Depression symptoms score, measured using the Patient Health Questionnaire eight item depression measure (PHQ-8)
• Sex, options are Male, Female, Prefer not to say, Other (please specify)
• Age, options from 18 to 81+ years old

Variables measured for each trial of the decision-making task:
• Response – which key (‘z’ or ‘m’) has been pressed
• Reaction time – time between stimulus presentation and key press response
indices The proportion of optimistic responses will be combined across both ambiguous stimuli to give each participant a single ‘proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli’ variable.
statistical_tests To determine whether there is an association between negative trait affect and pessimistic decisions to ambiguous stimuli, we will use a generalised linear model (GLM). The dependent variable will be the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli. The independent variables included in the model will be pessimism (LOT-R) score, anxiety (GAD-7) score, depression (PHQ-8) score, sex and age. We hypothesise a negative association between pessimism scores/anxiety scores/depression scores and the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli, therefore for each of these variables a negative beta coefficient and p < 0.05 will be treated as a significant result that confirms the corresponding hypothesis.

As we predict a degree of association between the independent variables related to negative trait affect (LOT-R, GAD-7 and PHQ-8 scores), we will also separately test for correlations between:

• Pessimism (LOT-R) scores and the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli
• Anxiety (GAD-7) scores and the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli
• Depression (PHQ-8) scores and the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli

This will be done using three separate GLMs, where the questionnaire score is the independent variable and the proportion of optimistic responses to ambiguous stimuli is the dependent variable. For each GLM, a negative beta coefficient and p < 0.05 will be treated as a significant result that confirms the corresponding hypothesis.
data_exclusion_criteria Data from participants who do not complete the whole experiment will be excluded. Data from participants who do not sufficiently complete the task, i.e. respond correctly on less than 50% of the unambiguous trials, will be excluded. Data from trials where the reaction times are too short (<200ms) or too long (>2000ms) will be excluded from the analysis.
exploratory_analyses To allow us to investigate how negative trait affect influences the decision-making process at the individual level, we will apply drift-diffusion modelling to the data.
